readerTitle: Your boss didn't read your update. Now what?
caseNote: 실제 연구 (Gabarro & Kotter, 1980 HBR) + 가상 사례 (대기업 내 팀, 냉난방 설비 서비스 회사)
insight: 상사 관리는 아첨이 아니라, 바쁘고 제약이 많은 상사가 나를 쉽게 도울 수 있도록 소식의 내용과 전달 방식을 상사의 목표와 습관에 맞추는 일이다.
misconception: 좋은 성과는 저절로 전달된다. 상사를 신경 쓰는 것은 정치이거나 비위 맞추기다.

sources.text: Gabarro, J. J., & Kotter, J. P. (1980). Managing Your Boss. Harvard Business Review.
대기업 내 팀(Dana)과 냉난방 설비 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Gabarro & Kotter(1980) 논문의 출간 연도와 제목, 핵심 주장(상사와의 관계는 상호 의존이며 의도적으로 관리해야 한다)을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요.
5번 카드의 목록은 논문 내용을 요약·의역한 것입니다. 특히 "읽는 쪽을 선호하는 상사 vs 듣는 쪽을 선호하는 상사" 구분(원래 Drucker의 표현을 인용한 것으로 알려짐)과 "Use their time well" 항목이 원문 취지와 맞는지 확인하세요.
6번 카드의 softwareNote(한 페이지 상태 공유가 긴 변경 기록보다 낫다)는 연구 결과가 아닌 일반적인 실무 조언으로 "tends to"로 표현했습니다.

cards.title: Your boss didn't read your update. Now what?
body: Every Friday, Dana sends her manager a careful two-page project update. Tables, risks, next steps.
On Tuesday, her manager is caught off guard in a leadership meeting: the project is two weeks late. That fact was on page two.
The work was fine. The way it reached the boss wasn't.

image.label: A long report on a phone screen, with one key line far down the scroll
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 회의실로 걸어가는 관리자가 스마트폰으로 긴 보고서를 엄지로 빠르게 넘기는 장면. 화면 아래쪽 멀리, 보이지 않는 위치에 빨간색으로 "2 weeks late" 한 줄. 실제 회사 로고나 앱 화면은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your manager keeps missing the key point.
body: You lead a small team inside a large company. Your manager keeps missing important points in your written updates, and she was just surprised in front of her own boss.
What's your next move?

options.text: Make the updates more thorough so nothing can be missed
options.feedback: More detail feels safer. But if she isn't reading past the first lines, a longer report buries the bad news even deeper.

options.text: Ask her how she likes to get news, and what her own boss asks her about
options.feedback: You spend one slightly awkward conversation and gain a channel that works. You also learn which news she can't afford to miss.

options.text: Put the biggest risk in the subject line from now on
options.feedback: A good fix for this one problem. But you're still guessing at what she needs and how she works.

cards.title: The report was written for someone who doesn't exist.
body: Dana's manager reads email on her phone, between back-to-back meetings. She skims the first lines and moves on.
Her own boss asks her one thing about this project: *will it ship on time?* So the one fact she needed most was the one buried deepest.
Dana wrote for a reader with a free hour and a quiet desk. Her real reader had ninety seconds and a hallway.

cards.title: Managing up
body: **Managing up** means deliberately working on your relationship with your boss so that both of you can do your jobs well.
It isn't flattery. It's treating your boss like any other important person you depend on: someone with goals, pressures and habits you can learn.
Your boss needs your results and honest news. You need their support, decisions and resources. When that exchange runs smoothly, you both win.

image.label: Two people linked by arrows: results and news one way, support and decisions the other
image.brief: 간단한 인포그래픽. 왼쪽에 "You", 오른쪽에 "Your boss". 위쪽 화살표(나→상사)에 "Results, honest news", 아래쪽 화살표(상사→나)에 "Support, decisions, resources". 두 화살표가 하나의 고리를 이루는 느낌.

cards.title: A relationship you manage on purpose
body: In a 1980 Harvard Business Review article, "Managing Your Boss", John Gabarro and John Kotter argued that the boss relationship is one of mutual dependence, and that effective managers manage it on purpose. Their advice comes down to a few habits:
list: **Learn their world:** goals, pressures, strengths, blind spots
**Learn their style:** some prefer to read, others to talk it through
**Know yourself:** how you react to authority, and where you clash
**No surprises:** bad news early, and from you
**Use their time well:** bring what they need to decide, not the whole story
cards.callout: Good work matters. It just doesn't deliver itself.

cards.title: It works whoever your "boss" is.
body: Not everyone has a manager. A business owner may answer to a bank, a landlord or one big client. A contractor answers to the homeowner.
The same habits apply. Learn what they worry about. Match how they like to hear news. Never let them be surprised by something you already knew.
cards.softwareNote: A product manager often manages up to several people at once: an engineering lead, a sales head, a founder. A shared one-page status with the date, the top risk and the decision needed tends to work better than a long changelog.

cards.title: Managing up is not managing around the truth.
body: It can slide into telling the boss only what they want to hear. That's the opposite of the idea. The goal is to make honest news easy to receive, not to soften it until it disappears.

It also takes time, and it isn't fully in your control. Some bosses won't meet you halfway. And if a boss's goals clash with what's right for customers or the company, adapting your style doesn't mean adopting their choice.

cards.title: Now it's a heating and cooling company.
body: You lead a crew at a family-run heating and cooling business. The owner is on job sites all day and hates long phone calls.
Today you find that a customer's ductwork is in worse shape than quoted. The job will run two days over, and the customer must approve extra cost. What do you do?

image.label: A technician in an attic texting, while the owner on a roof glances at her phone
image.brief: 화면을 둘로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽: 다락에서 낡은 덕트 옆에 선 기술자가 휴대폰으로 짧은 문자를 보냄. 오른쪽: 다른 현장 지붕 위에서 일하던 사장이 잠깐 휴대폰을 봄. 회사명이나 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

options.text: Finish today's work, then tell the owner at the end of the week
options.feedback: You avoid interrupting a busy owner, but she may hear it first from an unhappy customer. That costs far more trust than one text.

options.text: Text her now: the problem, the cost and time impact, two options, and your pick
options.feedback: It fits how she works and lets her decide in a minute. She hears the news early, from you, with a way forward.

options.text: Call her right away and walk her through everything you found
options.feedback: Early is right, and urgent news can justify a call. But a long call to someone on a roof gets half her attention. Lead with the decision you need.

cards.title: Make it easy for your boss to help you.
body: Your boss is a busy person with their own boss, goals and blind spots. Learn them, and shape your news to fit.
**Try it today:** ask your boss, or your most important client, one question: *What's the one thing you'd want to hear from me first, and how?*
